papers.title: The Effects of Jargon on Processing Fluency, Self-Perceptions, and Scientific Engagement
papers.study_kind: Randomized 2×2 between-subjects experiment with observational serial mediation
papers.scope: Full extracted paper pp.1–19, including methods, results, limitations, stimuli and references; actual DOI and year from p.1.
papers.sample_and_design: 650 paid U.S. Qualtrics panel adults randomized to jargon/no jargon and optional mouseover definitions/no definitions; each read three same-condition short science-technology passages (autonomous cars, surgical robots, 3D bioprinting). Jargon had 10 terms per paragraph; no-jargon replaced terms with explanations/synonyms; within-topic word counts held constant (pp.6–8).
papers.outcomes: Self-reported 1–7 processing fluency, science/technology self-schema, interest, information-seeking intention, internal efficacy, perceived knowledge. Not objective comprehension or actual behavior.

findings.claim: Jargon condition mean subjective fluency 4.57 (SD 1.11) vs 5.27 (0.90) without jargon; F(1,636)=76.03, p<.001, eta²=.11.
findings.interpretation_limits: Randomized bundle of term substitutions and acronyms; three short topics; self-reported fluency.

findings.claim: Definition availability: no main effect F(1,636)=0.37, p=.543 and no jargon interaction F(1,636)=0.17, p=.678.
findings.interpretation_limits: Null interaction is not proof of equivalence and mouseover access was optional.

findings.claim: Among 330 offered mouseover, 227 reported noticing it and 109 reported use (about 33% of 330); article calls it 31%. Of those aware, 109/227 ≈48%.
findings.interpretation_limits: Usage is self-selected; apparent arithmetic inconsistency noted, and unaware users were not asked.

findings.claim: Mean self-schema did not differ by jargon assignment alone, p=.590; unadjusted tests of four engagement outcomes were not significant (p=.165–.648).
findings.interpretation_limits: Modeled indirect pathways are not the same as randomized total effects.

findings.claim: Serial mediation indirect effects for interest 0.18 [0.12,0.25] and perceived knowledge 0.20 [0.12,0.28], unstandardized; 5,000 bootstrap resamples.
findings.denominator: participant-level outcomes; exact outcome-specific complete n not reported in table
findings.interpretation_limits: Mediators and outcomes were not independently randomized; authors explicitly say cross-sectional serial pathway is not causal.

limitations: Short, controlled, text-only immediate exposures; paid U.S. panel is not all audiences.
Definition treatment only offered hover access; 109/330 used by self-report. Findings do not show inline definitions are ineffective.
No objective understanding test; causal jargon manipulation does not identify causal serial mediation.
Appendix stimuli include technical claims that should not be treated as verified facts.
papers.data_or_code_leads: Online supplemental scale items mentioned p.8; no verified dataset or software release in full text.
extraction_issues: Paper describes 109 as 31% of 330; calculation is approximately 33%, retain original numerator and denominator.
Table 1 repeats some jargon cells unusually; do not use suspect topic rows for independent calculation.

papers.title: How Readability Shapes Social Media Engagement
papers.study_kind: Observational platform corpus plus randomized factorial experiment and related-platform follow-up
papers.scope: Full extracted paper pp.1–9, including both studies, follow-up, discussion, limitations and references; DOI/year from p.1 (online 2018, 2019 issue).
papers.sample_and_design: Study 1: 4,064 Humans of New York Facebook posts from 2013–2015; negative-binomial models with measured controls. Study 2: 236 MTurk adults randomized to 2 vocabulary complexity × 2 post lengths (59 versus 268 words) on a fictional running-shoe community post; synonyms manipulated with Dale–Chall list. Follow-up on HONY Twitter story excerpts may reuse stories and is not independent content replication (pp.2–7).
papers.outcomes: Actual Facebook likes, comments and shares; experimental self-reported willingness to like/comment/share, perceived ease, affect and reading time; Twitter likes/retweets. No comprehension or writing-quality test.

findings.claim: Field association uses 4,064 downloaded posts but table models report N=4,063. Higher Dale–Chall difficulty correlated with fewer likes/comments/shares, controlling measured covariates.
findings.interpretation_limits: Single social account, historical platform, unobserved post reach/audience/content confounding; association is not causal.

findings.claim: Observed readability × length interaction for likes and comments; share interaction p=.608.
findings.interpretation_limits: Conditional association; no universal length or reading-grade threshold follows.

findings.claim: Randomized simple vs complex post willingness-to-like: 4.33 (SD 1.69) vs 3.06 (1.81), F(1,232)=31.49, p<.001; complexity-by-length interaction p<.05.
findings.interpretation_limits: Intentions on one fictional running-shoe post rather than observed social behavior.

findings.claim: For short posts, comment p=.35 and share p=.45 did not differ significantly by complexity; long-post contrasts favored simpler wording.
findings.denominator: 236 randomized, cell sizes not reported in main text
findings.interpretation_limits: Do not read null as equivalence; experimental lengths differ substantially.

findings.claim: Processing fluency had no readability-by-length interaction p=.49; reading-time interaction p=.07; authors suggest long complex posts were abandoned.
findings.interpretation_limits: No direct measure establishes abandoning reading; p=.07 exploratory; mediators and affect not randomized.

findings.claim: Twitter follow-up used same HONY source, approximately 16 words on average, and reported readability associations with likes and retweets.
findings.evidence_locator: General Discussion, supplementary appendix S1 p.10
findings.denominator: Twitter post count not in main text
findings.interpretation_limits: Potential overlap in stories and photographs; supplement not inspected; no independent study-count claim.

limitations: Vocabulary familiarity is community-specific; authors explicitly discuss oversimplification and precision tradeoffs p.8.
One historical outlet and one hypothetical brand context; metrics do not measure argument quality or truth.
Laboratory outcomes are stated intentions, and proposed serial mediation does not establish a causal mediator chain.
Observational models do not resolve distribution/exposure confounding.
papers.data_or_code_leads: Facepager, VADER and IPTC taxonomy named pp.2–3; original snapshot and code not verified. Supplementary MDA Appendix S1 cited, not separately accessed.
extraction_issues: Abstract says >4,000; models N=4,063 versus sample 4,064.
Appendix statistics and actual Twitter post count were not in supplied main paper.

papers.title: Better Writing in Scientific Publications Builds Reader Confidence and Understanding
papers.scope: Full extracted paper pp.1–8, methods, results, discussion, data statement and references; DOI and publication date verified p.1.
papers.sample_and_design: 170 third-year undergraduate science participants from 173 approached read up to three randomized distinct-topic abstract variants; four predefined style levels bundle nine correlated manipulations for real-study-based abstracts in social anxiety, solar cells and populism. Models include topic and participant random intercept (pp.2–4).
papers.outcomes: 1–5 self-reported ease/readability and confidence; two topic-specific multiple-choice questions assess stated research purpose and take-home message. Comprehension is objective item correctness, not a broad competence test.

findings.claim: Analyzed 347 responses each for perceived readability/confidence (170 participants); understanding model 628 binary item responses from 143 participants.
findings.denominator: 347 reading events; 628 answer items; 170 vs 143 participants
findings.interpretation_limits: Repeated items are not independent participants and outcome denominators differ.

findings.claim: Difficulty composite model: readability +2.91 percentage points [1.79,4.03], confidence +1.87 [0.75,2.99] per unit toward accessible style; topic-adjusted mixed models.
findings.interpretation_limits: Style axis is PCA of a bundled manipulation; no individual component effect is isolated.

findings.claim: Understanding odds ratio 1.08 [1.01,1.15] per composite unit; p=.027, topic-adjusted mixed model.
findings.interpretation_limits: Two multiple-choice questions per abstract; odds ratio, not 8 percentage-point improvement.

findings.claim: Raw comprehension proportions nonmonotonic across easiest, easy, hard, hardest: 57.87%, 39.47%, 40.79%, 47.95%.
findings.denominator: 628 responses to understanding questions overall; per-level denominators not given
findings.interpretation_limits: Raw group proportions do not establish monotone dose-response; modeled result adjusts topic and reader.

findings.claim: No evidence of topic × difficulty or English-as-second-language effect in alternative models; authors caution sample not designed for ESL inference.
findings.interpretation_limits: Nonsignificance is not equivalence and subgroup sample is limited.

findings.claim: Table 2 reports easiest/hardest confidence 62.36%/48.78%; p.5 text instead gives 58.3%/44.1%, while discussion returns to 62%/49%.
findings.evidence_locator: Table 2 vs results prose and discussion
findings.denominator: 347 confidence responses; per-condition n not reported
findings.interpretation_limits: Unresolved internal discrepancy; avoid treating either contrast as independently verified.

limitations: Nine aspects vary together (including 0 hedges versus 4, acronyms, length, punctuation); isolated removal of any single feature is not tested.
Three created abstracts, student population, short testing and two questions limit domain and professional-reader generalization.
Results text and Table 2 differ on confidence means; Discussion p.6 inaccurately describes understanding as self-reported although methods explicitly describe multiple-choice scoring.
Authors retained content and logical flow by design, but whether all qualifications are equivalently represented is not independently audited.
papers.data_or_code_leads: Authors state raw data available on request p.7; supplementary abstract stimuli and alternative models linked in article. No code repository confirmed.
extraction_issues: Internal mismatch: Table 2 vs p.5 confidence means; retain both and no invented resolution.
Discussion p.6 calls all measures self-reported; methods and Tables 2–3 specify binary comprehension questions.
Table 3 confidence intercept appears extracted as 0.89 beside CI 66.30–75.47; not used.

cross_paper_synthesis: P01 manipulates wording and measures perceived processing ease, not objective comprehension; its serial mediation is observational. P05 combines historical behavior associations and randomized intent ratings; social engagement is not accuracy or utility. P09 randomized bundled styles and measured both perceptions and limited multiple-choice correctness.

Effects and targets depend on audience, task, vocabulary, topic and manipulation; numerical scales and denominators are not interchangeable. P09 does not isolate a style feature or justify removing qualifications.

The current skills already preserve precise technical terms and reject shorter-is-always-better. Existing audience-aware editing is common infrastructure; an advantage would need independent measures. The fresh F09 pilot showed 21/36 versus 18/36 exact set agreement and no semantic gold; this corpus cannot establish improved labels, function-length profiles or reader outcomes.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: skills/write-with-purpose/SKILL.md: familiar exact words; precise technical terminology; reader edit
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: A real unfamiliar or mixed-knowledge intended audience and a term whose interpretation is consequential.
proposed_rule_changes.candidate: Present a task-relevant technical term with the needed explanation in natural context or offer a more familiar accurate formulation; test both for the actual readers.
proposed_rule_changes.benefit: May reduce avoidable subjective difficulty while preserving technical distinctions.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: In specialist documentation, an exact established term can be more fluent and unambiguous than a vague paraphrase.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Record audience, declared terms and known glossary references; identify exact term occurrences only.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic: Decide whether the audience needs explanation, whether substitutes preserve meaning and whether scope remains accurate.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: skills/write-with-purpose/references/language-and-meaning.md: place brief definition naturally near the term
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: Definitions or optional glosses are introduced for readers new to a domain.
proposed_rule_changes.candidate: Assess visibility and use of definition in the reading flow; do not presume mere optional availability establishes comprehension.
proposed_rule_changes.benefit: Avoids a false completeness claim from existence of a glossary or hover.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A trained audience may not need an inline definition; mouseover failure cannot establish that inline teaching fails.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Check that supplied glossary entry and term link exist; log availability, not whether it was read.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic: Judge context, comprehensibility, precision and readers’ needs; measure uptake and comprehension separately.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: accepted-foundations.md F01–F06; edit-with-purpose/SKILL.md no automatic shortness
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: Reading metrics or engagement data are considered for revisions.
proposed_rule_changes.candidate: Treat readability indices and length as descriptive diagnostics scoped to audience and form; do not translate a score into a grade requirement or optimize engagement by default.
proposed_rule_changes.benefit: Makes tradeoffs visible without silently replacing author purpose.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A longer precise term or a longer complete explanation may be more accessible than a shorter obscure alternative.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Compute length or formula with stated tokenizer and word list; record source and scope.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic: Evaluate familiarity, goal alignment, accuracy and reader benefit; models cannot infer these from a numeric score.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: write-with-purpose/SKILL.md and language-and-meaning.md preserve uncertainty, qualifications, precision and voice
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: A bundled style recipe advises removing hedges, acronyms or making particular punctuation mandatory.
proposed_rule_changes.candidate: Reject component quotas; evaluate each qualification against evidence and preserve when it changes supported certainty or scope.
proposed_rule_changes.benefit: Avoids producing a confident but stronger or misleading claim.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A statistically warranted possibility cannot become a certainty to imitate a low-hedge experimental condition.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Flag changed modal/negation or removed declared term for review, with false positives.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic: Decide evidentiary force and meaning before approving edit.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: rule-calibration report; Astra candidate decision procedure; accepted F09 and measurement separation
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: Testing whether audience-aware assistance improves writing.
proposed_rule_changes.candidate: Run held-out audience-matched comparison with independent semantic fidelity, author acceptance and comprehension tests; separate readability feelings from performance and engagement.
proposed_rule_changes.benefit: Could test a differentiator in preserving nuanced content while adapting to actual readers.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A satisfying, fluent output may omit a key qualification or be factually wrong.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Blind and log assigned version, source IDs, decision status, data splits and score calculations.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic: Independent review of content, attribution, author authority and response quality.

github_reuse: Prior scientific-crosswalk records AZ, MuLMS-AZ and SciPara labels, units and cautionary mismatches. These can supply context examples and tests of attribution/defined terms, not labels for reader comprehension or universal templates.
No GitHub resource in these three papers was verified as a reusable reader-outcome benchmark. Reuse existing schema and rule comparisons without installing or claiming classifier validity.
open_questions: Which reader audiences and actual tasks matter for this author, and how can held-out samples represent them?
Can we preserve technical meaning and uncertainty while improving independently measured comprehension and retaining author voice?
Which definition placement works for a given reader and medium, as distinct from optional hover availability?
Can independent author and expert review establish semantic accuracy, not merely label agreement?
